When a ghost is discarded and proposed again under the same id, the fold lets the edges of the first proposal come back (found 2026-10-22: 10 stale refines/depends_on edges on 8 re-proposed ghosts, for example a second refines parent after a placement change).

**Why:** the fold keeps one edge list and filters it by whether the id exists. The id exists again, so the old `edge.added` events count again.

**How to apply:** after any discard-and-re-add, compare the card's outgoing refines and depends_on edges with what the new proposal intends, and `unlink` the extras on the ghost. An accepted card needs an amend instead. Also check that a card is still a ghost before `discard` (an accepted card needs `propose`, not discard). See [[feedback_siblings_are_not_evidence]] for why rewrites were done one card at a time.

card werk-mc-fork  [decided]
Fork the session, do not start it empty
why: Claude Code supports --fork-session. A fork keeps the shared prefix, so the cache still hits.

Confirmed. `--fork-session` hits the cache in full, and the parent is untouched.

## Method

`cd /tmp/werk-fork-proto` (scratch, outside this repo). Three `claude --print --output-format json` calls, same model:

1. A baseline turn carrying ~70k tokens of filler, no history.
2. A plain `--resume <session>` turn: a two-word reply, no new content.
3. A `--resume <session> --fork-session` turn: same, but forked.

## Result

    call        cache_creation_input_tokens   cache_read_input_tokens
    baseline    70118                         0
    control     61                            70118
    fork        61                            70179

The fork's `cache_read_input_tokens` (70179) equals the full prefix at the moment of the fork — the baseline plus the control turn, both already written to cache. It pays cache-read price for all of it and only writes 61 new tokens, the same number the plain control turn wrote for its own new content. A fresh, empty context would have paid full input price for that turn's own text and nothing else — cheaper in isolation, but it would then re-read every file and every card body the parent conversation already holds, on its own turns.

## What actually happens on disk

    ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/f35a3cc8-....jsonl   parent: baseline, control. Stops there.
    ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/29559e9c-....jsonl   fork: baseline, control, then its own FORK turn.

The fork is a full copy of the parent's history up to the fork point, under its own session id, as its own file. The parent file gains no fork turn — confirmed by reading both files after the run. So `resolveConvo` in src/convos.ts, which already keys off a session id, needs no change for this: a fork is just another session id with its own `chat.jsonl`.

## What this settles

- Werk's fork button should call `claude --resume <parent-session> --fork-session`, not start empty by default. #werk-mc-fork:opt0 stays the explicit second choice.
- The fold point for #werk-mc-shared's 'what changed since' question is exactly this: the last event each side saw as of the fork's parent-session read, which the log's `seq` numbers already carry.
- No further prototype needed here. The remaining unknown was fidelity of the cache hit under `--fork-session` specifically (as opposed to a bare new session), and it hit in full.

why: The output stream of a process can hold a line back in a buffer while the process goes on. If the fake wrote a file while its last event still waited in that buffer, a reader could get the event after the file was already on disk, and the order of the script would be lost.

To keep the order of a script visible to the reader, the fake agent plays an event step in two parts: it writes the line to its output stream, and it waits until the stream has taken the whole line. Only then does it play the next step.

Example:

- Event E1 "first", edit F "edited.txt", event E2 "second".

1. The fake writes E1 and waits until the stream has taken it. edited.txt does not exist.
2. The reader gets E1. edited.txt is still absent, if the script holds the fake here.
3. The fake writes edited.txt.
4. The fake writes E2. The reader gets E2, and edited.txt is on disk.

With no edit between two events, nothing changes: the reader gets the two events in order.

```
fake:    write E1 --wait--> write F --> write E2 --wait--> exit
reader:            get E1 (F absent)               get E2 (F present)
```

The wait covers the stream only. A test that must see the disk at E1 before F is written still holds the fake after E1, because the reader can be slower than the fake.

  -> refines         werk-v0-seams-fake-script  The fake agent replays a script of ordered steps: an event to print, or a file to write
  -> depends_on      werk-test-env  Tests never start the real agent or write to the real map
       why: The fake that this rule shapes is the one that the test run puts first in the program search list.

card werk-hmr-entry-settles  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
The command line's start-up finishes before a long verb runs, so a hot reload can start
why: Bun's hot reload does not run while the program's first evaluation still waits on something it loaded later. The serve verb runs until the server stops, so a start-up that waits for the verb's end would block every reload.

The start-up of the command line loads the verbs and starts the chosen verb. It does not wait for the verb's result as part of its own evaluation. The exit code is set when the verb ends, from a callback. So the first evaluation finishes at once, and a later edit of any module reloads it in the same process (see #werk-hmr for the runtime and the guard).

Example:

- The server runs under hot reload. The chat child C runs a turn.

1. The start-up loads the verbs, starts the serve verb, and finishes.
2. An agent saves an edit to a server module. Bun evaluates the modules again.
3. The serve verb finds the live server on the global object and swaps in the new request handler. C keeps its turn.
4. The person stops the server. The serve verb ends, and the callback exits with its code.

If the start-up waited for the verb, nothing would reload in step 2: the reload waits for an evaluation that never ends.

```
start-up:  load verbs -> start serve -> done
edit:      evaluate again -> swap handler    (C keeps its turn)
stop:      serve ends -> exit with its code
```

card werk-test-fake-ask-open-settle  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
A settled ask prints its tool result, and the turn ends at its first result event
why: A test must see when an ask settles and whether it was allowed. A real agent shows both by the tool result it prints after the answer. A denial is an answer like an allow, so it ends neither the turn nor the agent.

To show a settled ask the way a real agent does, the fake prints a tool result for it at the moment it settles. The tool result carries the id of the ask. An allowed ask gives a plain result. A denied ask gives an error result that says the tool was refused, and the script goes on. When the input channel closes before an answer arrives, no answer can come, so the ask settles as denied.

The end of the turn is the first scripted event of type result. A script with no such event ends its turn after its last step. At that point the fake waits for every open ask, then prints the result or exits.

A crash is its own step that holds an exit code. The fake exits with that code at once and prints nothing more.

Example:

- Ask A: a permission request for Bash, with id r1.
- Script S: ask A, a pause of 100 ms, a tool call, a final result.

1. The fake prints the request for A and goes on.
2. It stays silent for at least 120 ms, then prints the tool call.
3. It reaches the final result and waits for A.
4. The answer allow arrives. The fake prints the tool result for r1, then the final result.
5. With no input channel, step 4 is a denial: the tool result for r1 is an error, and the final result follows.
6. If S has a crash step in place of the tool call, the fake exits with its code after step 1, and nothing follows.

```
request r1 --> pause 120 ms --> tool call --> [wait for r1] --> tool result r1 --> result
request r1 --> crash(1) --> exit 1        (no tool result, no result)
```

card lp-overseer-silence-start  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
The silence clock starts at the agent's first event
why: An agent process takes time to start before it writes anything, and that time grows under load. Counting it as silence cancels a healthy agent when the silence limit is short. A start that never ends is still caught, by the wall-clock limit of the session.

The silence limit measures the time between two events of a session. Its clock starts when the agent writes its first event, and starts again at each event after that. Before the first event, only the wall-clock limit of the session applies.

Example, with a silence limit of 50 ms:

- Agent A "starts slowly": it takes 300 ms to start, then writes its first event, then nothing for 10 s.
- Agent B "runs a long tool call": it writes a tool call event at 300 ms, then nothing for 1 s, then the result.

1. A starts. 300 ms pass with no event. Nothing happens: the clock has not started.
2. A writes its first event. The clock starts.
3. 50 ms pass with no event and no tool call in flight. The overseer cancels A for silence.
4. B writes its tool call event. The clock starts, but a tool call is in flight, so the overseer waits.
5. B writes the result 1 s later. Nothing happens to B.

```
time (ms)   0        300        350               1300
A           start....event------X cancelled for silence
B           start....tool call=======in flight=====result
            .... = start-up, no clock   ---- = clock runs   ==== = tool call in flight
```

card werk-test-env  [decided]
Tests never start the real agent or write to the real map
why: A test that starts an agent must find the fake one, and a test must never write to a real project's log. Editing the search list for programs (PATH) in the test setup does not guarantee either, because Bun's process spawn, program lookup and shell read the environment the test process started with.

A unit test run isolates every test from the machine it runs on. Two things must not leak in. The first is the real agent: starting it costs money and time, and its answers change between runs. The second is the real project log: a test must never write to the map that a person is working in.

The run sets this up once, before the first test. It removes every variable that points at a real project, so a test has no way to reach the real log. It also puts the fake agent first in the program search list (the PATH variable), so a program lookup for the agent finds the fake before the real one.

Changing PATH inside the running test process is not enough. Bun's process spawn, its program lookup and its shell read the environment that the test process started with, not the environment as the setup edited it. A test that starts an agent without passing an environment of its own would still find the real agent. So the run also makes spawn, program lookup and the shell default to the cleaned environment. A process started by a test harness inherits the same cleaned environment.

The browser test server checks the same rule at start-up and refuses to start when the fake agent is not first in the search list. A leak then fails at once, not later as a surprise bill or a changed map. The browser harness uses the same fake agent as the command-line tests. With no script installed, that fake exits with an error.

why: The list of conversations must outlive the server that started them, and a restart gives the first tab a new session under the same tab name. One line per reported session keeps every past session listable, where one file per tab would overwrite the old session.

card werk-board-control-archive-ends-build  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
The builder loop ends its own build when it reads that its ticket is archived
why: A build can run from the merge loop or from a single build command, and only the builder loop is present in both. When the builder loop reads the board itself, an archive ends every build the same way, with no second process that has to notice it.

While a build runs, its builder loop reads the board about once a second. When it finds its ticket archived, it stops the agent of the pass that runs, commits nothing of that pass, runs no checks, records no retry, and ends. The worktree folder goes and the branch stays. A merge loop that started the build reads the ended build as a person's stop: nothing of it merges.

Example:

- Ticket T "Draw the board" is in building. Its pass 2 agent runs.
- A person archives T on the board.

1. The board log gets the archive. T leaves the columns.
2. Within about a second, the builder loop of T reads the board and sees T archived.
3. It stops the pass 2 agent. The session ends, so T stops pulsing.
4. The builder loop ends. Branch werk-build/T stays. Nothing merges.
5. Case where nothing happens: the person cancels the confirmation. No event, and the build goes on.

```
board log            builder loop of T            agent of pass 2
---------            -----------------            ---------------
T archived  ---->    reads board (~1 s): archived
                     stop  -------------------->  killed
                     no commit, no checks
                     worktree removed, branch kept
```

  -> refines         werk-board-control  A person reorders, archives, and triggers the build of one ticket at a time
  -> depends_on      st-build-ticket  The builder loop: one ticket, fresh passes until the checks, the grader, and the review pass

card werk-board-control-archive-ends-build  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
The builder loop ends its own build when it reads that its ticket is archived
why: A build can run from the merge loop or from a single build command, and only the builder loop is present in both. When the builder loop reads the board itself, an archive ends every build the same way, with no second process that has to notice it.

While a build runs, its builder loop reads the board about once a second. When it finds its ticket archived, it stops the agent of the pass that runs, commits nothing of that pass, runs no checks, records no retry, and ends. The worktree folder goes and the branch stays. A merge loop that started the build reads the ended build as a person's stop: nothing of it merges.

Example:

- Ticket T "Draw the board" is in building. Its pass 2 agent runs.
- A person archives T on the board.

1. The board log gets the archive. T leaves the columns.
2. Within about a second, the builder loop of T reads the board and sees T archived.
3. It stops the pass 2 agent. The session ends, so T stops pulsing.
4. The builder loop ends. Branch werk-build/T stays. Nothing merges.
5. Case where nothing happens: the person cancels the confirmation. No event, and the build goes on.

```
board log            builder loop of T            agent of pass 2
---------            -----------------            ---------------
T archived  ---->    reads board (~1 s): archived
                     stop  -------------------->  killed
                     no commit, no checks
                     worktree removed, branch kept
```

card werk-hmr  [decided]
Rebuild werk's dev server on a stack with HMR that survives its own edits
why: Research, two rounds of real-app testing, and a direct repro of the one open correctness concern settle it. Two priorities settle the rest: productionization and upgrade risk. See #werk-hmr:src0 through src5, and options opt1/opt2.
subtree: 3 cards, 3 decided

The agent's job includes editing werk's own source. A restart-based reload cannot support that: it kills the live claude child mid-turn every time the agent saves a file it is working through. Needs a stack where a code edit reloads the changed module without killing the process holding open child sessions.

Research (#werk-hmr:src0): vite-node invalidates transitively, not globally. Bun --hot guarantees the global object survives. Deno --watch-hmr names an in-flight async function as a forced-full-restart case, the exact shape of werk's failure. Node core has no HMR.

Toy prototype (#werk-hmr:src1): a minimal harness shaped like werk's agent, pinned on the global object, survived edits to both a sibling module and the pinned module itself, under both bun --hot and vite-node --watch.

Real-app test, unpatched (#werk-hmr:src2): werk's real code has neither guard. vite-node --watch crashed outright on an unrelated-file edit (an EADDRINUSE retry loop, then exit code 1). bun --hot did not crash, but silently orphaned a live task on the same edit.

Fix, real-app test, patched (#werk-hmr:src3): one guard clause in the server's start-up (a check, kept on the global object, that the server is not already running in this process) fixed both candidates identically. Both survive a real in-flight task through a source edit, verified with a fresh-connection check. Side effect worth knowing: this guard also means a hot reload stops applying code changes inside the start-up code - the tradeoff is 'my live session survives an edit' over 'my latest route-handler edit is live', which is correct for the original problem.

Runtime research (#werk-hmr:src4, Sept 2026): general research flagged one concrete objection to Bun as werk's runtime - oven-sh/bun #7716/#13811, open issues about SSE 'close' not firing reliably on client disconnect, which sounded like it hit werk's server directly.

Direct repro (#werk-hmr:src5): tested against Bun 1.4.1 specifically (the exact version used throughout, and the one the research flagged as the big Zig-to-Rust rewrite). Added a probe to werk's actual live-stream handler and disconnected SSE clients both cleanly and via kill -9. close fired correctly every time, the client left the server's client list, no leak. The bug is real and filed, but does not reproduce for werk's specific pattern.

Decided: move werk's runtime to Bun (bun --hot). The one concrete correctness objection did not reproduce on werk's own code on the exact version tested (1.4.1). The remaining Bun tradeoffs are a values call, not a correctness one, and two priorities resolve them: bun build --compile is a real asset for productionizing werk as a shipped tool (Node's own SEA docs mark it 'Stability: 1.1 - Active development', a weaker position), and Bun's faster breaking-change cadence is an acceptable cost given agents do the upgrade work rather than a single unaided maintainer. #werk-hmr:opt2 records staying on Node as the rejected alternative; #werk-hmr:opt1 records the original Bun rejection, superseded once #werk-hmr:src5 tested it directly.

card lp-overseer-inflight  [decided]
The overseer tells a working tool call from a frozen one
why: A test that waits on a promise that never resolves, or an I/O call to a resource it cannot reach, looks the same as a long build from outside. Only the process shows the difference.
subtree: 3 cards, 3 decided

Two sources show a tool call that is still running:

1. The tool-call stream. A call that has started and has no result yet is in flight. The overseer knows the tool, its input, and its start time.
2. The operating system. A shell call is a process tree. For each process the overseer reads the CPU time, the state, the output written, and the open files and network connections.

Together they tell working from frozen:

| CPU time | Output | Open connections | Reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| grows | any | any | working |
| flat | grows | any | working |
| flat | flat | one, to a host that does not answer | frozen on I/O |
| flat | flat | none | frozen on a wait that never ends, such as a promise that never resolves |

"Flat" means no change for 60 seconds, the same starting value as #lp-overseer-silence. The first runs show whether it needs to change.

A frozen call is cancelled. The agent gets the cancel as the call's result, with the evidence, and continues.

The watch covers every agent session that can run a tool, not only the builder: the grader, the reviewers, and the held-out binder (#lp-heldout-binder) too. The binder is the session that needs it most. It runs the whole held-out suite, often end-to-end browser tests, and that run prints nothing for minutes. Without the watch, the silence limit cancels it mid-run and every step comes back not run.

A test runner with a per-test timeout catches most frozen tests first. The overseer catches what the runner does not: a hang outside any test, a runner with no timeout, or a command that is not a test.

card werk-mc-recall  [decided]
A tab lists its sibling conversations and reads any one of them
why: werk already stores every conversation's session id. It can point straight at the file the prior-conversations skill would have to search for.

Built.

## What it does

One operation lists every conversation with its home card, session id, turn count, and last activity. A second operation resolves a reference — a conversation name, a session id or prefix, or a card id — to one transcript and prints it. An ambiguous card id is an error, not a guess: two conversations on one card is a mistake worth seeing.

A search takes case-insensitive patterns and may repeat. A message must match all of them. The messages on each side of a hit can print with it.

## The two sources, both wired

Default is werk's own chat transcript. Tool calls and results are in it but hidden unless asked for, because they are most of the file.

The raw mode reads Claude Code's own transcript through the prior-conversations skill's script. No second parser. That script already strips system-reminder noise and finds the file from a session prefix. If it is not installed, the raw mode fails with the transcript's own path so the work is not blocked.

## The prototype question, answered by building both

There was no need to choose. werk's transcript is the default because it is clean and already card-tagged; the raw transcript is one flag away when a flattened `Edit` label hides the answer.

## Forward layout

The list reads `.werk/conversations/<name>/{session,chat.jsonl}`, and also lists today's single conversation — `.werk/session` plus `.werk/chat.jsonl` — under the name `main`. So this works before #werk-multichat exists and keeps working after, with no migration.

## The prompt side

The agent's system prompt tells it these operations exist and, more importantly, tells it never to answer 'I have no access to the other conversation'. That is a launch flag, so a running child keeps the old prompt until it restarts.

card werk-mc-fork-notice  [decided]
A fork keeps the parent's model and links back to the fork point
why: A fork is a continuation. A different model and a chat with no origin both make it look like a new conversation.

## Model

A fork starts on its parent's model and advisor, not on the default. `ConvoManager.fork()` copies `modelSetting()` to the new agent before its first start.

## Notice

The fork's chat opens with one system line: "Continued from <parent>." It carries `forkOf: {convo, at, session}`.

- `at` is the time of the parent's last `you` or `agent` message at the moment of the fork.
- The pane renders a "Go to the last message before the fork" button. A click switches to the parent tab, scrolls to that message, and outlines it for a short time.
- Each message node carries `data-at`, so the button finds its target.
- If the message is older than the 200-line history window, the button only switches tabs.

## Restart

`session` and the notice's `card` let a fork that never sent a message survive a server restart. `describeConvo` reads them back as `home` and `forkFrom`, so the first send still forks the parent.

The model is not on disk for any conversation. After a server restart, a rebuilt fork falls back to the default model, the same as every other tab.

  -> depends_on      werk-resume  A restart resumes the conversation

card werk-chat-fake-role  [decided]
The fake agent lives as long as the agent it stands in for
why: A chat agent and a build pass both read their messages from an open input stream. The chat agent answers many messages, and a build pass answers one and ends. A fake with the wrong life hangs a test or hides a bug in how werk ends a pass.

A chat agent and a build pass take their input the same way, so the fake cannot tell them apart by how it is started. werk tells the fake which kind of agent it stands in for (see #st-build-seam-role-env).

- **Chat agent.** One conversation lives across many messages (see #werk-onechat). Each message is one turn: the fake records it, plays the next scripted reply, and waits. It ends when its input closes.
- **Any other agent.** One pass does one unit of work and exits (see #lp-stateless). The fake reads the first message, plays one reply, and exits with the code of the script. A permission answer that arrives on the input is part of that reply, not a new turn (see #werk-test-fake-ask-open).

Example:

- C is a chat agent. Its script has two replies, R1 and R2.
- B is a build pass. Its script has one reply, R1, with one permission ask, and exit code 0.

1. A test sends message M1 to C. C plays R1 and waits.
2. The test sends M2 to C. C plays R2 and waits.

card lp-heldout-binder  [decided]
A binder agent turns steps into tests, and never makes a test pass
why: The binder reads the code. If it may change a test until it passes, it fits the test to the code, and the held-out set checks nothing.

The binder reads the merged code, finds the elements each step names, and writes the tests for the project's stack.

Two rules.

1. The binder cannot change step text. It only maps each step to UI actions and assertions.
2. The binder does not make a test pass. When a step fails, it records the failure and stops. It fixes only its own errors, for example a typo in a locator.

"Element not found" can be a binder error or a missing feature. The binder reports which one it thinks it is, and the coordinator reads that report.

Example of what rule 2 stops: search does not update live. A binder that may make tests pass adds a page reload before the search. The test passes and the feature is still wrong.

Rule 2 is enforced after the session, not trusted: a binder that changed any file outside its own test directory has fitted the product to the test, and its whole report is void. Everything the binder and its test runner write inside that directory is its own, whatever the file names — screenshots, traces and result folders included. A path is compared as stored, never as a display form that quotes or escapes unusual characters, or the binder's own output reads as a change to the product and voids a correct report.

Accepted risk: a binder writes a wrong test, and a correct feature fails. This is fixed when it happens, not prevented.

card werk-chat-fake-role  [decided]
The fake agent lives as long as the agent it stands in for
why: A chat agent and a build pass both read their messages from an open input stream. The chat agent answers many messages, and a build pass answers one and ends. A fake with the wrong life hangs a test or hides a bug in how werk ends a pass.

A chat agent and a build pass take their input the same way, so the fake cannot tell them apart by how it is started. werk tells the fake which kind of agent it stands in for (see #st-build-seam-role-env).

- **Chat agent.** One conversation lives across many messages (see #werk-onechat). Each message is one turn: the fake records it, plays the next scripted reply, and waits. It ends when its input closes.
- **Any other agent.** One pass does one unit of work and exits (see #lp-stateless). The fake reads the first message, plays one reply, and exits with the code of the script. A permission answer that arrives on the input is part of that reply, not a new turn (see #werk-test-fake-ask-open).

A card stays at the level of the decision. It may name behaviour, concepts, and the commands and flags a person types (`werk run`, `--unchallenged`). It must not name source files, functions, classes, constants, line numbers, or internal HTTP endpoints. A card about a code module names the module by its role ("the conversation manager"), not its file.

**Why:** Eryk stripped these from ~60 amended cards (2026-10-09): implementation names go stale with every refactor while the decision still holds. The code points to the card, not the reverse. The rule is on #werk-wording.

**How to apply:** when writing or amending any card (including audit-driven fixes that "make the card match the code"), describe the behaviour, not where it lives. Evidence like file:line belongs in chat, not in the card. Related: [[cards-are-about-themselves]], [[pipeline-cards-generic]].

card werk-chat-fake-role  [decided]
The fake agent lives as long as the agent it stands in for
why: A chat agent and a build pass both read their messages from an open input stream. The chat agent answers many messages, and a build pass answers one and ends. A fake with the wrong life hangs a test or hides a bug in how werk ends a pass.

A chat agent and a build pass take their input the same way, so the fake cannot tell them apart by how it is started. werk tells the fake which kind of agent it stands in for (see #st-build-seam-role-env).

- **Chat agent.** One conversation lives across many messages (see #werk-onechat). Each message is one turn: the fake records it, plays the next scripted reply, and waits. It ends when its input closes.
- **Any other agent.** One pass does one unit of work and exits (see #lp-stateless). The fake reads the first message, plays one reply, and exits with the code of the script. A permission answer that arrives on the input is part of that reply, not a new turn (see #werk-test-fake-ask-open).

Example:

- C is a chat agent. Its script has two replies, R1 and R2.
- B is a build pass. Its script has one reply, R1, with one permission ask, and exit code 0.

1. A test sends message M1 to C. C plays R1 and waits.
2. The test sends M2 to C. C plays R2 and waits.
3. The test closes the input of C. C exits.
4. werk sends the prompt P to B. B plays R1 and prints the ask A.
5. werk sends the answer to A. B does not start a new turn. B finishes R1 and exits with 0.

```
C (chat)                      B (build pass)
M1 --> R1, wait               P  --> R1 ... ask A
M2 --> R2, wait               answer A --> (same turn)
input closed --> exit         R1 done --> exit 0
```

card werk-base  [decided]
v0 is a new project, built from scratch in its own repository
why: The current code is a prototype, iterated on to find the right shape. v0 is the clean implementation of that shape.
subtree: 3 cards, 3 decided

v0 starts in a new, empty repository. Nothing is ported from the prototype code.

- The spec is the decided cards that #werk depends on, not the prototype code.
- The prototype code is a reference. A builder may read it to see how a decided behaviour looks. It does not copy it.
- The stack is #werk-stack: React + Vite for the client, inside the Bun server from #werk-hmr. Vite transforms the client, so v0 has a client build step.

Why not extend the prototype: it works well as a product, but its code is messy. A clean build tests whether the decided cards are enough to rebuild the behaviour.

The kill criterion for this choice is recorded on #werk. The prototype's behaviour sets the bar. The fallback is to extend the prototype code (see the option on this card).

  -> refines         werk  werk v0
  -> depends_on      werk-stack  werk's client is built from components on one framework
       why: v0 is built on the stack that #werk-stack chose.
  -> depends_on      werk-hmr  Rebuild werk's dev server on a stack with HMR that survives its own edits
       why: v0 uses the Bun server with hot reload that #werk-hmr chose.
  <- alternative_to  werk-base:opt2  Extend the prototype code until each v0 item works
  <- refines         werk-base-dir  v0 grows in its own directory beside the prototype, with its own packages and checks
  <- refines         werk-base-repo  v0 is built in a new git repository whose main branch starts with zero files
Options
  werk-base:opt2  Extend the prototype code until each v0 item works
    why not: The prototype code was written to find the shape, not to keep. Extending it carries every shortcut into v0.

See #werk-base for why v0 is a new project.

card lp-overseer-psfail  [decided]
A failed process probe leaves a running call unknown, not frozen
why: A probe that cannot read the process table gives no evidence about the call. Reading its empty answer as a frozen call with no process cancels a pass that may be working.
subtree: 2 cards, 2 decided

When the process probe cannot read the process table, the overseer treats the sample as unknown. The sample does not count toward the flat CPU time of #lp-overseer-inflight, and it cancels nothing.

The probe tells a failed read apart from a read that found no process. Only a read that ran can report that a call has no process of its own.

**What still stops a real stall.** While a tool call runs, the silence rule of #lp-overseer-silence does not fire. So during a probe failure, the only stop is the wall-clock cap on the pass (#al-sample-budget). A stalled pass runs to that cap, not to the 60-second mark.

**The cost, stated.** A real stall during a probe failure costs up to one full cap of time and tokens. Cancelling instead costs a pass that may be working, and charges the ticket a retry for a fault in werk's own probe.

The overseer records each failed probe as an event. A pass that ends at the cap then shows that the probe was blind.

  -> depends_on      al-sample-budget  Every verb that runs claude goes through one clamp: N at most 5, wall clock at most 900s

One ticket, one worktree.

card werk-mc-shared  [decided]
Cross-tab memory is pulled from the session logs, not pushed into context
why: A stale sibling is fine. When one conversation needs another, it searches the session log on disk instead of being fed a diff.
subtree: 2 cards, 2 decided

A fork that does not know what its sibling said is not a bug to fix. It is the normal state, and the fix is a search, not a broadcast.

Two channels, both pull, neither push:

1. **State — the map.** Tab A's context can say #x is open while tab B decided it. That is harmless, because no agent answers from its context: it reads the card from the map before it writes. The map on disk is always current. Every turn already works this way, so it needs no new mechanism.

2. **What was said — the session log.** `~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>.jsonl`, one file per session, complete, including turns compaction dropped. The `prior-conversations` skill exists for exactly this, and it handles the hard part: it groups worktrees by git origin and strips tool noise.

    SCRIPT=~/.claude/skills/prior-conversations/scripts/convo-search.py
    python3 "$SCRIPT" search "keyword" "another"
    python3 "$SCRIPT" show <session-id> --grep "keyword" --context 3

werk can do better than that skill, and should. The skill guesses which session to read from keywords. werk *knows*: it stores the session id for every conversation itself. So it can hand the agent an exact list of sibling conversations and their home cards, and skip the search-and-hope step. See #werk-mc-recall.

What this rejects: feeding a tab a 'here is what changed since your fork' diff on focus. See #werk-mc-shared:opt0.

  -> refines         werk-multichat  Several conversations at once, in tabs
  -> depends_on      werk-mc-fork  Fork the session, do not start it empty
       why: Cross-tab memory assumes tabs are forks of one session that diverge, as this card decides.
  -> supported_by    vi-overwrite  A turn edits cards in place, so the map shows only the current state
  <- alternative_to  werk-mc-shared:opt0  Push a 'what changed since your fork' diff into a tab when it gets focus
  <- refines         werk-mc-recall  A tab lists its sibling conversations and reads any one of them
  <- refines         werk-mc-shared-convo-log  Each conversation session is one line in an append-only conversations log beside the map log
Options

    why not: It pays on every switch for something that is needed on a few of them. It also fights the tool's own model: the map on disk is the current state, so an agent that reads a card before writing it is never wrong, whatever its context believes. A diff would only be re-telling the agent something it can look up. Pull beats push here because the need is rare and the lookup is exact.

card werk-mc-split  [decided]
A conversation has a home card, not a subtree boundary
why: Focus is a label, not a fence. A conversation crosses subtrees whether you allow it or not.

The two obvious options are 'arbitrary split' and 'per-subtree focus'. Neither fits. The third:

A conversation records the card that was open when it started. That id is its name, its tab label, and the seed context sent on its first turn. It is not a fence. The conversation may navigate anywhere, and the pane keeps sending the open card on every turn.

Why not a real subtree fence: a conversation that opens at #root can end up writing under #werk-chat. A fence would block it or force a switch. The map's tree is where a card sits; it is not where a thought stays.

What the home card buys, with no fence:
- The tab reads '#werk-mc-fork' instead of 'Chat 3'.
- Two tabs on the same home card are visibly a mistake.
- The fold can compute what changed under that card since the fork point. See #werk-mc-shared.

  -> refines         werk-multichat  Several conversations at once, in tabs
  -> depends_on      werk-mc-fork  Fork

card lp-heldout-mechanics  [decided]
The builder never sees the held-out steps
why: The held-out set only works if the builder cannot see it and the binder cannot make a feature look present.

- One step author per ticket. It runs with no tools; the program stores its answer under .werk/heldout/<run>/. A follow-up ticket gets no step author.
- The binder binds every step of the run in a temporary worktree. If it changes a file outside .werk-heldout/, its whole report is void.
- A binder error files no follow-up. The set runs once more at the end of the run; an error that stays ends the run as heldout and waits for a person.
- One held-out run files one follow-up for all newly failed steps. A step that an open follow-up already carries files no second one.
- The red badge stays on the merged ticket after its follow-up goes green.

Known gap: the builder's Read tool can reach .werk/heldout/ by an absolute path. The steps are out of the builder's worktree, not out of its reach.

  -> depends_on      lp-heldout-author  A step author writes the steps from the brief, in parallel with the builder

  -> depends_on      lp-heldout-binder  A binder agent turns steps into tests, and never makes a test pass
       why: The mechanics enforce the binder rules of this card, so the binder cannot make a feature look present.

card st-heldout-notrun  [decided]
A held-out step the binder could not run is not run, not red
why: A binder that timed out or failed says nothing about the product. Showing it as red reports a break that nobody found.

After a merge, each held-out step ends green, red, or not run. A step is not run when the binder session failed, hit its time limit, or could not bind the step.

A not-run step files no follow-up ticket. On the board it shows as a grey badge on the done ticket, apart from the red badge of a step that ran and failed (#werk-board-columns). G2 still waits for it, because it is not green: the next held-out run after a later merge tries it again.

The binder's time limit grows with the number of steps it has to bind, so a large set does not time out where a small one would pass.

  -> depends_on      werk-board-columns  The board follows the whole run, with one column per ticket state

### werk-resume [card decided] parent=werk-onechat
TITLE: A restart resumes the conversation
WHY: Editing werk means restarting werk. A fresh session would lie: the transcript stays on screen.
The child reports its session id in the `system/init` event. werk writes it to `.werk/session` and passes it to `--resume` on the next start. Verified: told the agent a codeword, killed the server, restarted, and it answered from the resumed session.

The failure path matters as much. A stored id that no longer resolves makes the child report an error result and exit before it ever reaches init. werk detects that, clears the id, starts a new session, and **replays the message you were waiting on**. Verified.

One bug found while testing this: the error result cleared the pending message before the exit handler ran, so the replay had nothing to send. A result that arrives before init is not a finished turn.

A person can start a fresh conversation on purpose.

### werk-edits [card decided] parent=werk-pane
TITLE: The pane may edit code with no prompt
WHY: An edit that waits on a prompt stalls the turn, and editing werk's own code is the agent's normal work.
Edit and Write are in the default tool allowlist, and the child runs in the auto permission mode (#werk-perm-mode). A file edit applies with no prompt. A call that auto cannot resolve arrives as an ask in the pane (#werk-approve).

The cost: the pane can write to any file in the repository, and the pane shows no diff. Use git to see what changed. A server flag narrows the allowlist.

### al-diff-cli-btn [card decided] parent=vi-onview
TITLE: Accept is a button. Discard is a typed correction
WHY: A pending card has a ✓ button that accepts the proposal. Discard has no button, because the user steers a bad proposal by telling the agent.
A `✓` icon button sits in the top-right row of buttons on a card with a pending proposal. A click asks the server to accept. The server checks that the card still has a pending proposal. Then it appends the same accept event as an accept from the command line.

Discard has no button. The user corrects a bad proposal by telling the agent what is wrong, and the agent proposes again. Only accept needs no chat, because it ends the review.

### werk-context-pie-fork [card decided] parent=werk-context-pie
TITLE: Fork inherits the parent's context reading
WHY: 
Two bugs, both from the same root cause: a forked tab's Agent object exists before its child process ever starts, and contextUsed stays its constructor default (0) until the first real turn reports usage.

1. **Pie showed 0% right after a fork**, even though the forked session already carries the parent's full history — #werk-mc-fork confirmed the cache hit is real, so the tokens are real too. Fixed: ConvoManager.fork() now passes the parent's current context() into the child Agent's constructor (initialContext), so the pie reads the inherited size immediately, before any turn runs.

2. **Clear context did nothing before the first message.** clearContext() cleared the session file and the transcript, but never touched forkFrom — the in-memory pointer a pre-first-message fork uses instead of a session file. So the next send still forked the parent. Fixed: clearContext() now also sets forkFrom = null, so clearing before the first message produces a genuinely empty conversation.

card st-build-run-mechanics  [decided]
The merge loop drives one run: a temporary merge worktree, a guarded branch move, and a stop when a build stays red
why: The merge loop has to be safe to resume and must never overwrite a run tree that moved under it.

- Starting the merge loop on a planned subtree is the person's trigger for its tickets. Starting it again resumes.
- The merge queue merges the ticket's branch in a detached worktree and runs the ticket's own checks there.
- The main line moves only from the value it had when the merge started, so a main line that changed in between is never overwritten (#st-plan-main). A checkout of the main line moves with it by a fast-forward. A checkout whose local changes block that fast-forward stops the loop, and nothing moves.
- After a red merge, the next build starts from the ticket's old branch when that branch sits on top of the main line.
- A ticket's retry cap counts passes across all its builds, so it also bounds the trips between the builder and the merge queue.
- A build that stays red stops the loop as stuck.
- Every start of the loop writes the feature tier event to the board log first (#werk-loop-tier).
- G2 belongs to the main line's tip: a later merge opens it again. Only a person passes it (#st-gates).

The open-card announcement has no recovery path once it drops from context
why: A whole visible conversation can run with the map open at one card while the agent is never told. The last announced card is state in the long-lived server process, set before the agent's visible context began. There is no tool for the agent to ask which card is open.

The full card description was sent only when the open card changed (per #werk-pane). If the change happened before the agent's visible context — a resumed session, or a turn dropped by compaction — the agent had no way to learn or re-derive the open card. The full card description still goes only on a change; every other turn gets a one-line '[still on #id — title]' reminder, cheap enough to send always. ### werk-invoke [card decided] parent=werk-pane
TITLE: A spawned claude subprocess speaking stream-json, not the Agent SDK
WHY: werk needs one long-lived local child, resumable, bound to this repo's log — chosen when werk-pane was first built, but never written down or checked against the alternative.
Four ways to run Claude Code programmatically. Two don't fit werk's shape at all:

- Managed Agents (hosted REST API) — Anthropic runs the sandbox. No local child, no access to this repo's working tree.
- Client SDK (raw Anthropic API) — you write the whole tool loop yourself. Throws away every built-in tool, hook, and session feature Claude Code's own harness already gives werk for free.

Two genuinely apply, and werk picked one without writing down why:

- Headless CLI (-p / --print), what agent.ts does — spawn the claude binary, talk newline-delimited stream-json over stdin/stdout. src/agent.ts hand-parses that protocol itself: assistant/user/result/stream_event, --resume, --model, --advisor, tool_use blocks. Every wire-format detail agent.ts knows about is public API surface werk maintains against.
- Agent SDK (Python or TypeScript library) — same tools, same agent loop, same session/hook/subagent machinery, but as an in-process library call (query() / ClaudeSDKClient) instead of a subprocess. Would replace most of agent.ts's hand-rolled parsing with the SDK's own message objects, and would turn --permission-prompt-tool's MCP round-trip into an in-process canUseTool callback (see werk-approve). Not adopted: nothing currently broken forces the rewrite, and werk is already committed to the stream-json wire format working — switching is a rewrite for its own sake, not a fix.

Worth re-opening if: the hand-rolled parsing in agent.ts breaks against a new Claude Code version, or the werk-approve research on canUseTool/PermissionRequest turns up something the CLI truly cannot do.

A restart resumes the conversation
why: Editing werk means restarting werk. A fresh session would lie: the transcript stays on screen.

The child reports its session id in the `system/init` event. werk writes it to `.werk/session` and passes it to `--resume` on the next start. Verified: told the agent a codeword, killed the server, restarted, and it answered from the resumed session.

The failure path matters as much. A stored id that no longer resolves makes the child report an error result and exit before it ever reaches init. werk detects that, clears the id, starts a new session, and **replays the message you were waiting on**. Verified.

One bug found while testing this: the error result cleared the pending message before the exit handler ran, so the replay had nothing to send. A result that arrives before init is not a finished turn.

A person can start a fresh conversation on purpose.

card werk-test-runner-parallel  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
The unit tests run on parallel workers, with a per-test time limit that allows for the shared load
why: A test run in one process takes most of the time that the build loop gives one check, so a slow machine fails the check for time alone. Parallel workers cut the run to about a third. But the workers compete for the machine, and a test that starts many processes then runs past a short per-test limit.

To keep the unit test run well inside the time limit of one check, the test command runs the test files on four workers at the same time. Each test gets a default limit of 15 seconds instead of the runner default of 5 seconds. A test that needs more still sets its own, longer limit. The limit is not a gate on speed: a test that hangs still fails, only later.

       why: takes the rule that a check is one command whose run the loop ends at a time limit

**`bun test` for everything in-process. `@playwright/test` for everything in a browser.**

`bun test` is already in the runtime from #werk-hmr. Jest-style `expect`, watch mode, and `--coverage` are built in, and it adds no runner dependency. `bun run test:coverage` runs it with lcov output, then a coverage gate enforces the 90% line on each pure module in #werk-test-scope.

card werk-mc-park-unpark  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
An un-park keeps a live process, and resumes a stopped one at once
why: A parked conversation whose process still runs has lost nothing, so a restart would only cost time. A conversation whose process was stopped must be back before the person types, so the resume starts at the click and not at the next message.

The page tells the server each time a conversation is parked or un-parked. Only the server knows whether the conversation's process still runs. To avoid a second process for one conversation, an un-park of a conversation with a live process changes nothing on the server. To avoid a wait at the next message, an un-park of a conversation with no live process and a known session starts a new process at once, on that session with the resume option. A conversation with no session yet starts nothing, and its first message starts a fresh process as before. Any later process of a conversation that has a session also resumes that session.

Example: conversations A and B, and B has session s-b.
1. B is parked. Its process still runs. The person clicks B in the '…' menu. B's chip comes back, and no process starts.
2. B is parked again and stays idle past the idle limit. The check kills its process.
3. The person clicks B in the menu. The server starts a process with the resume option and s-b.
4. A has never sent a message and is un-parked. No process starts.

```
un-park B
  live process?  yes -> keep it            (step 1)
                 no  -> session known?  yes -> start: --resume s-b   (step 3)
                                        no  -> start nothing          (step 4)
```

The server reads two optional values when it starts. WERK_IDLE_MS is the idle limit: how long a parked conversation may stay idle before its process is killed. It defaults to 30 minutes. WERK_IDLE_CHECK_MS is the time between two idle checks. It defaults to 60 seconds, or to the idle limit when that is shorter. A value that is not a positive whole number is ignored, and the default holds.

Example: a server starts with WERK_IDLE_MS=300. A conversation is parked and has no open turn. About 300 ms later, the next check kills its process. With no value set, the same conversation keeps its process for 30 minutes.

WERK_IDLE_CHECK_MS  unset -> min(60000, idle limit)

## How to fix it in place

A ghost is frozen. The only correction is: discard, then propose again with the same id.

All WRITE commands go through the lock wrapper, because many reviewers write at the same time
and the log has no lock of its own:

```
/tmp/werk-w discard <id>
/tmp/werk-w add <id> --title "..." --why "..." --body "..." --parent <id> --status open --who <w>
/tmp/werk-w link <from> <to> --type depends_on --why "..."
/tmp/werk-w unlink <from> <to> --type <t>
/tmp/werk-w add <id>:opt0 --kind option --title "..." --why_not "..."
/tmp/werk-w link <id>:opt0 <id> --type alternative_to
/tmp/werk-w status <id> decided
/tmp/werk-w kill <id> ...
```

Read commands (`show`, `find`) may use `node src/cli.ts` directly.

Procedure for a rewrite:

1. Right before the discard, run `show <id>` again. If it no longer says PROPOSED, Eryk
   accepted it meanwhile: do NOT discard. Stage the change with `/tmp/werk-w propose <id> ...`
   instead (see `node src/cli.ts --help`), or report only.
2. Write down every outgoing edge, every option (with why_not), the who, the status, and any
   kill criterion. A discard takes the ghost options with it.
3. Discard, then `add` the whole card in one call. Re-add the options you keep, re-link them,
   re-link depends_on with their reasons, and set the status the card had (a `decided` status
   needs the contract: who, depends_on or --no-basis, an option or --unchallenged for who:you,
   a kill criterion — copy the old criterion).
4. Run `show <id>`. A discard then re-add revives the old edges. Unlink every edge the new
   proposal does not intend (a second refines parent, a dropped depends_on).
5. Bodies with backticks, quotes or newlines: build the arguments safely, for example
   `--body "$(cat /tmp/body-<id>.md)"` from a file you Write. Do not edit any repo file.

Rules for scope:

- Touch ONLY your own card and its own options. Never discard, edit or link FROM another card.
  You may add a depends_on or alternative_to edge FROM your card TO another card.
- Never run `accept`. Never `remove` a card.
- If the card is not worth keeping, or should merge into another card, do NOT discard it.
  Fix nothing and report the recommendation; Eryk decides.
- If the card is fine, change nothing and say so.
- Do not touch `.werk/*.wgrid` and do not start sysdiag agents.
- Do not ask Eryk anything. Do not use `say`.

## Report (your final message, under 350 words)

```
ID: <id>
VERDICT: keep | keep-after-fix | merge-into <id> | change-to-existing <id> | split | drop
CHANGED: <what you changed on the map, or "nothing">
PLACEMENT: <parent now, and why>
CONTRADICTIONS: <card-id vs card-id: the two statements>, or none
CODE CHECK: <matches | mismatch: what>
DECISION FOR ERYK: <the one question he must answer about this card, with 2 options if it is a choice, or "accept as is">
```

The silence limit measures the time between two events of a session. Its clock starts when the agent writes its first event, and starts again at each event after that. Before the first event, only the wall-clock limit of the session applies (see #al-sample-budget).

Example, with a silence limit of 60 s and a wall-clock limit of 600 s:

- Agent A "starts slowly": under load it takes 90 s to start. It writes its first event, then stops.
- Agent B "runs a long build": it writes a tool call event at 5 s. The build runs for 300 s, then the result comes.
- Agent C "never starts": it writes no event at all.

1. 90 s pass with no event from A. Nothing happens: the clock of A has not started.
2. A writes its first event at 90 s. Its clock starts.
3. 60 s pass with no event and no tool call in flight. At 150 s the overseer cancels A for silence.
4. B writes its tool call event at 5 s. Its clock starts, but a tool call is in flight, so the overseer waits.
5. B writes the result at 305 s. Nothing happens to B.
6. C writes nothing. At 600 s the wall-clock limit cancels C.

```
time (s)  0        90       150          305           600
A         start....event----X
B         start=tool call (5 s)=in flight==result
C         start.....................................X
          .... = start-up, no clock running
          ---- = silence clock running
          ==== = tool call in flight, overseer waits
          X    = cancelled: A for silence, C at the wall-clock limit
```
EOF

10959:The page tells the server each time a conversation is parked or un-parked. Only the server knows whether the conversation's process still runs. To avoid a second process for one conversation, an un-park of a conversation with a live process changes nothing on the server. To avoid a wait at the next message, an un-park of a conversation with no live process and a known session starts a new process at once, on that session with the resume option. A conversation with no session yet starts nothing, and its first message starts a fresh process as before. Any later process of a conversation that has a session also resumes that session.

A fork carries the parent's whole history (see #werk-mc-fork). That is wrong for an unrelated topic. To give that topic a clean start, the tab strip has a second control next to '+' (see #werk-mc-open for '+'). The empty control opens a new tab at the open card, with no parent session. The first message in that tab starts a session with no history. No other gesture starts a conversation empty.

The empty control never switches to an existing tab. A fork switches to a tab that already has the card as its home. The empty control opens a new tab every time, also on that card. The new tab still takes the open card as its home and its chip label (see #werk-mc-split).

Example:

- tab "main", home card "#map", active. The map shows "#fold".
- tab "fold", home card "#fold".

1. The person Shift+clicks a link to "#fold". The pane switches to tab "fold". No tab opens.
2. The person goes back to "main". The map shows "#fold" again.
3. The person presses the empty control. A second "#fold" chip opens and becomes active. Its conversation has no history.

    start:              [#map*] [#fold]           +  ∅
    Shift+click #fold:  [#map]  [#fold*]          +  ∅   (switch, no new tab)
    ∅ on #fold:         [#map]  [#fold] [#fold*]  +  ∅   (new tab, no history)

    *  the active tab
    +  the fork control
    ∅  the empty control
EOF

TITLE: A tab's background agents are the last list of background tasks its agent reported
WHY: Claude Code resends its whole list of background tasks each time one starts or ends. Reading the last list, not counting starts and ends, cannot drift when one event is missed. A child that exits takes its background tasks with it.
To tell a finished main turn from an idle tab, the conversation manager keeps the number of background tasks that the agent's last task list named. A tab runs while a turn is open or that number is above zero. When the child exits, the number drops to zero.

### werk-mc-live-dead [card GHOST] parent=werk-mc-live
TITLE: A child that exits without werk stopping it marks its tab dead until the tab's next child starts
WHY: Werk stops children on purpose, by the idle sweep and at shutdown, and those exits must not read as deaths. Any other exit needs a decision from the person, so the mark and the line in the other panes stay until a new child replaces the dead one.
A child is dead when it exits and werk did not stop it. A stop by the idle sweep, or by the server as it shuts down, is not a death. To keep the mark honest, a death also drops the open asks and the background agents of that child: nobody can answer them any more. The mark stays until the next child of that tab starts, on the next message or on an un-park. While it stays, every other tab's pane shows one line under its chat log that names the dead tab and gives the error.

Example:
- tab #fold "Fold the cards from the log", in the background, with an ask open
- tab #log, in focus

1. The agent of #fold exits with code 1. The #fold chip turns red, and the ask leaves its ask bar.
2. The #log pane shows the line: #fold died: the agent exited with code 1.
3. The person focuses #fold. Its own pane shows the error at the end of its turn, and no line.
4. The person sends a message in #fold. A new child starts, the chip is no longer red, and the line leaves every pane.
5. The idle sweep stops a parked tab's child. Nothing turns red, and no line shows.

A fork of a tab with no session opens an empty tab
why: A fork copies the session of the tab it comes from, and a tab that has never sent a message has none. Opening the tab anyway keeps the fork gesture working on every tab. The new tab then behaves like an empty conversation on the clicked card.

A fork copies the session of the tab it comes from. A tab that has sent no message, and is not itself a fork, has no session. To keep the fork gesture from failing on such a tab, the fork opens the new tab anyway, on the clicked card, with no parent session. Its first message starts a new session with no history. The new tab keeps its home card (see #werk-mc-split).

A tab that is itself an unsent fork still has a session to copy: the one it will resume. A fork of that tab copies the same session, so it does not start empty.

Example:

- tab A, homed on "#map", has sent no message and is not a fork.
- tab B is a fork of A at "#fold".

1. The person forks A at "#fold". Tab B opens with home "#fold" and no parent session.
2. B sends its first message. Its agent starts a new session, with no history.
3. The person forks a tab that already has a session. Nothing changes from the normal fork: the new tab copies that session.

A child that exits without werk stopping it marks its tab dead until the tab's next child starts
why: Werk stops children on purpose, by the idle sweep and at shutdown, and those exits must not read as deaths. Any other exit needs a decision from the person, so the mark and the line in the other panes stay until a new child replaces the dead one.

A child is dead when it exits and werk did not stop it. A stop by the idle sweep, or by the server as it shuts down, is not a death. card st-heldout-followup-per-ticket  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
A red held-out run files one follow-up ticket for each ticket whose steps went red
why: A held-out run covers the steps of every done ticket in the subtree. When every red step goes into one follow-up ticket, that ticket mixes unrelated work from many tickets. One hard step then holds back every easy one, and the cap stops them all together.

Each held-out step belongs to the ticket whose steps file holds it. To keep one hard step from blocking unrelated fixes, a red run groups its red steps by that ticket and files one follow-up ticket per group. Each follow-up cites the cards of its own source ticket, and it has its own retry cap. A source ticket that already has an open follow-up gets no second one; its new red steps wait for the next run.

Example:

- Tickets P and Q are done. Run R turns step P.2 red, and steps Q.1 and Q.4 red.

1. R files follow-up F1 with step P.2, citing the cards of P.
2. R files follow-up F2 with steps Q.1 and Q.4, citing the cards of Q.
3. F2 stops at its cap. F1 still builds and merges.
4. A later run turns Q.1 red again while F2 is open. No new ticket is filed for Q.

```
run R:  P.2 ✗   Q.1 ✗   Q.4 ✗
         │        └───┬───┘
         ▼            ▼
        F1 (P)       F2 (Q)      ✗ = red step, (X) = source ticket
```

Three states, not one, and two of them do more than mark.

1. **Running.** A pulsing dot on the tab chip and on the card elsewhere in the tree that the conversation is homed on. Passive: confirms the turn is still going. Per #werk-mc-bgagents: a background agent counts as running too — a tab whose main turn finished but that still has a background agent going must not read as idle.
2. **Waiting for input.** The conversation has a queued permission ask. Per #werk-mc-asks: the tab's own dot blinks yellow, and the '...' button blinks yellow too if the waiting tab is hidden behind it. No shared queue, no line in another tab's pane.
3. **Dead.** The child process exited. #werk-fullerr and #werk-crashmsg decide what the message says and when a retry is safe, for a single conversation. Neither one asks *where* that message goes when the dying conversation is not the one in focus. Decided here: a background death is not something you find by chance. It surfaces the same way an ask does — a visible line in the pane, naming the tab, not buried behind a dot you'd have to notice on your own.

So the marker itself is three-state (running / waiting / dead). 'Waiting' signals through the dot and the '...' button, per #werk-mc-asks. 'Dead' pushes a line into whatever pane you're looking at. To keep every past session listable, the server appends one line to a conversations log in the same folder as the map log. It appends the line each time a tab's agent reports a session id that the log does not hold yet. A line holds the tab name, the session id, the home card when the tab has one (see #werk-mc-split), and the parent session when the tab is a fork (see #werk-mc-fork). No line is ever rewritten. The list of conversations folds the lines into one entry per session id.

A plain restart resumes the same session and adds no line (see #werk-resume). A tab gets a new session under its old name only when its stored session no longer resolves at a start, or when the server starts the first tab fresh on purpose. In those cases the old session stays in the log.

Example. These things exist:

- Tab main, whose agent reports session s-1.
- Tab map-hash, a fork of s-1 with home card #map-hash, whose agent reports session s-2.

1. Tab main reports s-1. The log gains the line main s-1.
2. Tab map-hash reports s-2. The log gains the line map-hash s-2, home #map-hash, parent s-1.
3. The server restarts and tab main resumes s-1. The log gains nothing, because it holds s-1 already.
4. At the next restart s-1 no longer resolves, so tab main reports a new session s-3. The log gains the line main s-3.
5. The list shows three conversations: s-1, s-2 and s-3. Both s-1 and s-3 carry the tab name main.

```
step  event                          line appended to the conversations log
1     main reports s-1          -->  main      s-1
2     map-hash reports s-2      -->  map-hash  s-2  home #map-hash  parent s-1
3     restart, main resumes s-1 -->  (none: s-1 is in the log already)
4     restart, s-1 is gone,
      main reports s-3          -->  main      s-3

list:  s-1 (main)   s-2 (map-hash)   s-3 (main)
```
EOF

card ms-fail-cause  [decided]
A rerun of the red check sets the flaky cause. The next builder pass sets the other causes
why: The next pass already reads the failure and the code to fix it, so it knows the cause with no extra session. Only flakiness needs no judgement: the same check on the same commit either passes again or does not.

The cause names are those of #ms-fail.

- **Flaky.** A red check runs once more on the same commit. Green on the rerun gives the cause flaky. The pass stays red: the rerun classifies, it does not change the verdict.
- **Check infrastructure.** The check reports a crash, a timeout, or a missing tool before the code ran. The check run sets this cause itself, with no judgement, and the check is not run again. A stop by the person is not a check infrastructure fail.
- **Every other cause.** The next pass names one cause of the last failure, with one sentence of reason, at the end of its work. Conflict applies only to a fail from the merge loop.
- **No next pass.** A fail at the retry cap has no next pass, so its cause stays unknown.

The cause is stored on the pass that named it, and the report attributes it to the pass before. A cause the check run set comes before a cause the next pass names.

card werk-mc-live-dead  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
A child that exits without werk stopping it marks its tab dead until the tab's next child starts
why: Werk stops children on purpose, by the idle sweep and at shutdown, and those exits must not read as deaths. Any other exit needs a decision from the person, so the mark and the line in the other panes stay until a new child replaces the dead one.

A child is dead when it exits and werk did not stop it. A stop by the idle sweep, or by the server as it shuts down, is not a death. To keep the mark honest, a death also drops the open asks and the background agents of that child: nobody can answer them any more. The mark stays until the next child of that tab starts, on the next message or on an un-park. While it stays, every other tab's pane shows one line under its chat log that names the dead tab and gives the error.

Example:
- tab #fold "Fold the cards from the log", in the background, with an ask open
- tab #log, in focus

1. The agent of #fold exits with code 1. The #fold chip turns red, and the ask leaves its ask bar.
2. The #log pane shows the line: #fold died: the agent exited with code 1.
3. The person focuses #fold. Its own pane shows the error at the end of its turn, and no line.
4. The person sends a message in #fold. A new child starts, the chip is no longer red, and the line leaves every pane.
5. The idle sweep stops a parked tab's child. Nothing turns red, and no line shows.

cat > /tmp/body-werk-hmr-entry-settles.md <<'EOF'
Bun's hot reload waits until the first evaluation of the program ends. A verb that runs until someone stops it, such as serve, never ends. To keep reloads working, the start-up of the command line starts such a verb and does not wait for it. The verb reports a failure, and sets the exit code, from a callback when it ends. So the first evaluation ends at once, and a later edit of any module reloads it in the same process (see #werk-hmr for the runtime and the guard). A short verb, such as add or show, may still be awaited, because it ends before anyone edits a file.

Example:

- The server runs under hot reload. The chat child C runs a turn.

1. The start-up loads the verbs, starts the serve verb, and ends.
2. An agent saves an edit to a server module. Bun evaluates the modules again.
3. The serve verb finds the live server on the global object and swaps in the new request handler. C keeps its turn.
4. The person stops the server. The server stops its children and exits.

If the start-up waited for serve, nothing would reload in step 2. The reload waits for an evaluation that never ends, and the edit has no effect until a restart.

```
start-up:  load verbs -> start serve -> end      (no wait on serve)
edit:      evaluate again -> swap handler        (C keeps its turn)
stop:      server stops C -> exit
```
EOF

card werk-board-control  [decided]
A person reorders, archives, and triggers the build of one ticket at a time
why: Build order is a person's choice while the process is iterative (#st-iterative), and a manual trigger keeps that choice in their hands.
subtree: 3 cards, 3 decided

Four direct actions on the board:

1. Reorder tickets within ready.
2. Archive a ticket. A ready, blocked or building ticket shows this action; a merging or done ticket does not. Archiving a building ticket ends its build and keeps its branch. Archiving asks for confirmation first, and the confirmation says the ticket is never deleted for good — an agent can restore it, the same reversible pattern #werk-remove already uses for a map card.
3. Trigger the build of a ready ticket inside an active run. Either press the trigger icon, or drag the ticket into building.
4. A triggered build cannot be stopped in place. A person ends it by archiving its ticket (action 2), and nothing else returns a building ticket to ready.

The drag from ready into building is the only manual column-to-column move. Every other move is not a person's call:

- Ready and blocked: an agent moves the ticket, and always either states the blocking reason or resolves it.
- Building, merging, and done: the merge loop moves the ticket (#st-build-run). A red check in merging sends it back to building automatically, never by a manual drag.

A plan is the one actor besides a person that archives: it archives an open ticket that the subtree's current spec no longer needs, with that reason, and a restore puts it back (#st-plan-archive).

Nothing builds before a person starts the run. Starting the merge loop on a plan run is the person's trigger for the whole run (#st-build-run). Inside an active run, the board trigger starts one ready ticket early. That ticket builds, then goes through the same merge queue: building, merging, done. Up to 3 tickets build at once (#st-build-parallel).

A ticket is not edited on the board. A person asks an agent to change it, and the agent runs the ticket-set checks again (#st-ticket).

       why: Manual ticket reordering and triggering exist because build order stays a person's choice in the iterative process this card defines.

card ms-fail  [decided]
Each failed pass records which gate failed it, and the cause
why: A pass count says how often the loop failed, not what to fix. A fail from a spec gap needs a plan fix, and a fail from a flaky check needs a check fix. Neither is a builder mistake.
subtree: 2 cards, 2 decided

**Gate.** Each fail names its gate: a check by name, such as type check, lint or unit test (#lp-checks); the grader, with the card the diff failed against (#lp-prod-judge); a review area, with the finding's severity (#lp-prod-review); or the merge loop, for a conflict with another ticket (#st-build-run). A gate that judged nothing — a stalled or looping pass, a broken step — is named too, and has no cause.

**Cause.** Each fail gets one cause:

- *builder error*: an earlier pass got the code wrong, and the spec was clear. The gate says whether it broke a check or missed the spec, so one cause covers both.
- *test is wrong*: the test asserts old behaviour, and the diff is right. Only a check or a merge fail can have it.
- *spec gap*: the spec does not say what the diff should do.
- *false finding*: the finding passes on the next pass with no change to the code it names.
- *check infrastructure*: the check crashed, timed out, or lacked its tool, and the code did not run.
- *flaky*: the check passes on a rerun with no change to the code.
- *conflict*: the ticket clashes with work merged after it was built. Only a merge fail can have it.

#ms-fail-cause says who sets each cause.

**Derived numbers.** The first-pass success rate, the cap-hit rate (the share of builds that reach the retry cap, #st-build-ticket), the passes per build as median, 90th percentile and maximum, and the fails by cause and by gate. A build is one run of the builder loop over one ticket. A ticket that the merge loop sends back builds twice, and each build counts on its own.

**Starting thresholds.** These are guesses until data exists. Each needs a minimum sample, so that one bad build does not fire it.

- A cap-hit rate above 10%, over at least 10 builds, points at ticket size or spec quality, not at the builder.
- One gate key that fails three builds in a row becomes a check or a rubric line (#ms-rubric).
- A false-finding share above 20% for one reviewer or the grader, over at least 5 of its fails, means its prompt needs a fix.
- Any flaky or check-infrastructure fail is a fix to that check, not to the builder.

### st-spec-decisions [card decided] parent=st-spec
TITLE: The spec and ticket writers return their own decisions as data; the program proposes the cards
WHY: An agent that adds cards itself can write a card nobody can trace to the plan step. Data the program reads can be checked first.
Each writer writes every answer that no card gives to a JSON file beside the spec: id, title, why, body. The program reads the file and proposes a card for each entry, under the planned subtree, with who me. A card it cannot add is reported with the reason. The writers' own tools are Read, Grep, Glob and Write.

### st-build-ticket-order [card decided] parent=st-build-ticket
TITLE: A builder pass: checks stop at the first red, then the grader, then the review
WHY: The cheap verdict runs first. A grader or reviewer that breaks must not let a pass through.
1. The checks run in order and stop at the first red one.
2. The grader runs only on green checks. It scores the decided cards of the ticket's depends_on closure (#lp-prod-judge); a card it leaves out scores 0.
3. The five reviewers run only on a passing grade. An unknown severity counts as MEDIUM and does not block.
4. A broken or silent grader or reviewer fails the pass as a failed step, with the reason in the next brief.

A silenced builder pass still commits its edits, skips the checks, and counts against the cap. A ticket whose build ends red stays in building. Each build writes one card obligation (#st-build-card); an unsatisfied obligation does not block the build.

### lp-heldout-mechanics [card decided] parent=lp-prod-heldout
TITLE: The builder never sees the held-out steps
WHY: The held-out set only works if the builder cannot see it and the binder cannot make a feature look present.
- One step author per ticket. It runs with no tools; the program stores its answer under .werk/heldout/<run>/. A follow-up ticket gets no step author.
- The binder binds every step of the run in a temporary worktree. If it changes a file outside .werk-heldout/, its whole report is void.
- A binder error files no follow-up. The set runs once more at the end of the run; an error that stays ends the run as heldout and waits for a person.
- One held-out run files one follow-up for all newly failed steps. A step that an open follow-up already carries files no second one.
- The red badge stays on the merged ticket after its follow-up goes green.

Known gap: the builder's Read tool can reach .werk/heldout/ by an absolute path. The steps are out of the builder's worktree, not out of its reach.

Three conflicts in a row still mark the ticket stuck (#st-build-stuck-park says what stuck stops).

WHY: 
WHY_NOT: The rebuild costs a full build, and every merge that lands during it can conflict with it again. A list that every ticket appends to conflicts on each try.


### st-heldout-beside [card decided] parent=st-build-run
TITLE: The held-out set runs beside the merge queue, and the next merge does not wait for it
WHY: The held-out set grows with every merged ticket. While the merge queue waits for it, the green branches behind it age and conflict.
After a merge, the held-out set starts on that merge's commit in the background. The merge queue takes the next ticket at once. A red step files a follow-up for the ticket whose merge it ran after, as #st-validate-heldout sets.

When a held-out run is still going and a newer merge lands, the older run is not stopped: each result belongs to its own commit. Only the result on the main line's final tip opens G2 (#st-g2-heldout).

986:**How it runs Claude Code.** Conductor starts its own pinned claude binary as a child process, through a sidecar runtime. The child's stdin, stdout and stderr are unix sockets to the sidecar, not a terminal. One user turn is one JSON line written to stdin, in stream-json format. Conductor never pastes text and never simulates keystrokes. Because the sidecar owns that stdin, no other program can write into a Conductor session.
988:**How it stores events.** Each session has one outbox file. The file holds a version, the session id, a next-sequence counter and a list of pending events. Each pending event wraps the raw stream-json payload with a session id, a turn id and a user-message id. The queue drains into a SQLite database.
