The start-up of the command line starts a verb that runs until someone stops it, such as serve, and does not wait for it. The verb reports a failure, and sets the exit code, from a callback when it ends. So the first evaluation ends at once, and a later edit of any module reloads it in the same process (see #werk-hmr for the runtime and the guard). A short verb, such as add or show, may still be awaited, because it ends before anyone edits a file.

Example:

- The server runs under hot reload. The chat child C runs a turn.

1. The start-up loads the verbs, starts the serve verb, and ends.
2. An agent saves an edit to a server module. Bun evaluates the modules again.
3. The serve verb finds the live server on the global object and swaps in the new request handler. C keeps its turn.
4. The person stops the server. The server stops its children and exits.

If the start-up waited for serve, nothing would reload in step 2. The reload waits for an evaluation that never ends, and the edit has no effect until a restart.

```
start-up:  load verbs -> start serve -> end      (no wait on serve)
edit:      evaluate again -> swap handler        (C keeps its turn)
stop:      server stops C -> exit
```

  -> refines         werk-hmr  Rebuild werk's dev server on a stack with HMR that survives its own edits

card werk-test-dom  [decided]
Component tests share one DOM for the whole unit run
why: Server tests and React component tests run in one process and need different globals, and React finds a DOM only if one exists when it first loads.

This is the way werk meets #werk-test-globals. One DOM window is registered before any test file loads, so React finds a DOM when it first loads. The network, stream and timer globals of the runtime are put back after the registration, so a server test in the same run uses the real network function, not the one of the DOM. Each component test unmounts what it rendered.

The test runner and the client framework that this rests on are chosen in #werk-test-runner.

  -> refines         werk-stack  werk's client is built from components on one framework
  -> depends_on      werk-test-globals  Each test runs with the globals that its own code expects
       why: The single shared DOM is the way werk meets the rule that each test sees its own globals.
  -> depends_on      werk-test-runner  One test runner, or one per side
       why: The DOM is registered for the bun test runner that #werk-test-runner chooses, with React from the same card.
  <- alternative_to  werk-test-dom:opt0  Register a DOM per component test file and remove it after the file
  <- refines         werk-test-dom:opt0  Register a DOM per component test file and remove it after the file
Options
  werk-test-dom:opt0  Register a DOM per component test file and remove it after the file
    why not: React finds a DOM only when it first loads in the process. A DOM registered later, or removed and registered again for each file, is not the one React already holds, so only the first file would be safe. The shared DOM also costs one registration, not one per file.
card ms-fail-cause  [decided]
A rerun of the red check sets the flaky cause. The next builder pass sets the other causes
why: The next pass already reads the failure and the code to fix it, so it knows the cause with no extra session. Only flakiness needs no judgement: the same check on the same commit either passes again or does not.

The cause names are those of #ms-fail.

- **Flaky.** A red check runs once more on the same commit. Green on the rerun gives the cause flaky. The pass stays red: the rerun classifies, it does not change the verdict.
- **Check infrastructure.** The check reports a crash, a timeout, or a missing tool before the code ran. The check run sets this cause itself, with no judgement, and the check is not run again. A stop by the person is not a check infrastructure fail.
- **Every other cause.** The next pass names one cause of the last failure, with one sentence of reason, at the end of its work. Conflict applies only to a fail from the merge loop.
- **No next pass.** A fail at the retry cap has no next pass, so its cause stays unknown.

The cause is stored on the pass that named it, and the report attributes it to the pass before. A cause the check run set comes before a cause the next pass names.

card lp-overseer-silence-start  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
The silence clock starts at the agent's first event
why: An agent process takes time to start before it writes anything, and that time grows under load. Counting it as silence cancels a healthy agent when the silence limit is short. A start that never ends is still caught by the wall-clock limit of the session.

The silence limit measures the time between two events of a session. Its clock starts when the agent writes its first event, and starts again at each event after that. Before the first event, only the wall-clock limit of the session applies (see #al-sample-budget).

Example, with a silence limit of 60 s and a wall-clock limit of 600 s:

- Agent A "starts slowly": under load it takes 90 s to start. It writes its first event, then stops.
- Agent B "runs a long build": it writes a tool call event at 5 s. The build runs for 300 s, then the result comes.
- Agent C "never starts": it writes no event at all.

1. 90 s pass with no event from A. Nothing happens: the clock of A has not started.
2. A writes its first event at 90 s. Its clock starts.
3. 60 s pass with no event and no tool call in flight. At 150 s the overseer cancels A for silence.
4. B writes its tool call event at 5 s. Its clock starts, but a tool call is in flight, so the overseer waits.
5. B writes the result at 305 s. Nothing happens to B.
6. C writes nothing. At 600 s the wall-clock limit cancels C.

```
time (s)  0        90       150          305           600
A         start....event----X
B         start=tool call (5 s)==========result
C         start........................................X
          .... = start-up, no clock running
          ---- = silence clock running
          ==== = tool call in flight, overseer waits
          X    = cancelled: A for silence, C at the wall-clock limit
```

/**
 * The conversation manager (#werk-chat, #werk-chat-stdin, #werk-invoke). Each conversation
 * tab has one Claude Code child in the chat role, spoken to over stream-json. The child lives
 * across many messages: each message is one more user line on its stdin, one turn.
 *
 * The child runs one turn at a time. The manager keeps the turns that were sent and have not
 * ended, in the order they were sent, and gives each part of the reply to the oldest of them.
 * The end of a turn closes it, and the next one starts (#werk-chat-turn-id). A child that exits
 * ends every open turn with the exit, so no turn waits forever, and the next message starts a
 * new child.
 *
 * Each tab keeps its session id, from the init event of its child, and its home card
 * (#werk-mc-split). A tab opened from another tab records the session of that tab at the
 * moment it opens: the fork point. Its child then starts on that session with the fork
 * option, so it shares the parent's cached prefix and leaves the parent untouched
 * (#werk-mc-fork). A tab opened empty, or from a tab that has no session yet, has no parent
 * session, and its child starts a new one. The first turn of an opened tab names its home card.
 *
 * A tab can be parked (#werk-mc-park). Its child lives on: a parked tab is not closed. An idle
 * check runs every `checkMs` and kills the child of each parked tab that has had no turn open
 * and no agent activity for `idleMs` (#werk-mc-reap, #werk-mc-reap-sweep). A message wakes the
 * tab. Each child after the first of a tab with a session resumes that session (#werk-resume),
 * and an un-park of a tab whose child is gone starts that resumed child at once
 * (#werk-mc-park-unpark).
 *
 * The manager reports a status per tab to the status sink each time it changes (#werk-mc-live):
 * running while a turn is open or a background agent of the child runs (#werk-mc-bgagents),
 * the first permission ask of the child that has no answer, and dead from an exit that werk
 * did not cause until the tab's next child starts. A tab keeps its own asks, and an answer goes
 * to that tab's child alone (#werk-mc-asks). A child that exits takes its asks and its
 * background agents with it.
 *
 * Each new session a tab's child reports goes to the session sink, so the conversations log
 * lists it (#werk-mc-shared-convo-log). Nothing a tab says reaches another tab's child: a tab
 * reads a sibling from its transcript when it needs it (#werk-mc-shared).
 */

The page tells the server each time a conversation is parked or un-parked. Only the server knows whether the conversation's process still runs. To avoid a second process for one conversation, an un-park of a conversation with a live process changes nothing on the server. To avoid a wait at the next message, an un-park of a conversation with no live process and a known session starts a new process at once, and that process resumes the session (see #werk-resume). A conversation with no session yet starts nothing on un-park. Its first message starts a fresh process.

Example: conversations A and B. B has the session s-b. A has never sent a message.
1. B is parked. Its process still runs. The person clicks B in the '…' menu. B's chip comes back, and no process starts.
2. B is parked again and stays idle past the idle limit. The idle check kills its process (see #werk-mc-reap).
3. The person clicks B in the menu. The server starts a process at once, and it resumes s-b. The person types into a conversation that is already running.
4. A is un-parked. No process starts. A's first message starts a fresh process.

```
un-park B
  live process?  yes -> keep it, start nothing              (step 1)
                 no  -> session known?
                          yes -> start now, resume s-b      (step 3)
                          no  -> start nothing              (step 4)
```

### werk-mc-tabs [card decided] parent=werk-multichat
TITLE: A tab strip of card-id chips, in the bottom control cluster
WHY: Tabs at the bottom, connected like real tabs, flush to the pane edges.
Settled by iterating on the running app, not by discussion — three rounds of feedback on the
same build:

1. Placement: the strip is its own row, last in the pane — the chat log, the dead-child bar, the asks,
   the chat header row (state · context pie · model select), the composer, then the tab strip. The
   model/context/state row sits above the composer, not attached to the tabs.
2. Shape: a chip is a real tab, not a button. The strip carries one shared top border; the
   active chip erases its own piece of that line by matching the pane's background (`#11161d`,
   the same color the composer above it already shows through to), so it reads as attached to
   whatever is above rather than floating below it. An inactive chip keeps a full border and a
   lighter panel fill so it visibly sits apart until clicked.
3. Edge-to-edge: no horizontal padding on the strip. Tabs start flush at the pane's left edge,
   the way a browser's own tab strip does, instead of sitting indented inside a margin.

### werk-crashmsg [card decided] parent=werk-resume
TITLE: Never blame the session for a crash it did not cause
WHY: Any early exit was read as a dead session, so werk deleted a working conversation.
The first version treated *any* exit before `init` as proof that the stored session id was bad. It cleared the id and started over. A transient crash therefore destroyed a perfectly good conversation, and the pane said only "The agent exited (code 1)" with no reason.

Three changes.

1. Only `No conversation found with session ID` clears the id. That string comes from Claude Code itself. Anything else leaves the id alone, because losing a working conversation costs far more than one retry.
2. The child's stderr is kept and shown. "code 1" became "error: option '--permission-mode <mode>' argument 'nonsenseMode' is invalid. Allowed choices are acceptEdits, auto, bypassPermissions, manual, dontAsk, plan."
3. One automatic retry, then "Your message was not delivered. Send it again." A crash loop cannot spin, and a message is never silently dropped.

Verified both paths. A planted dead id is cleared and the message replays into a new session. An invalid permission mode crashes twice, reports the real reason, and the good session id survives and still resumes.

The start-up of the command line loads the verbs and starts the chosen verb. It does not wait for the verb's result as part of its own evaluation. When the verb ends, a callback exits with the verb's exit code. So the first evaluation ends at once, and a later edit of any module reloads it in the same process (see #werk-hmr for the runtime and the guard).

Example:

- The server runs under hot reload. The chat child C runs a turn.

1. The start-up loads the verbs, starts the serve verb, and ends.
2. An agent saves an edit to a server module. Bun evaluates the modules again.
3. The serve verb finds the live server on the global object and swaps in the new request handler. C keeps its turn.
4. The person stops the server. The serve verb ends, and the callback exits with its code.

If the start-up waited for the verb, nothing would reload in step 2. The reload waits for an evaluation that never ends.

```
start-up:  load verbs -> start serve -> end      (no wait on serve)
edit:      evaluate again -> swap handler        (C keeps its turn)
stop:      serve ends -> callback -> exit with serve's code
```
EOF

cat > /tmp/body-werk-test-runner-parallel.md <<'EOF'
To keep the unit test run well inside the time limit of one check, the test command runs the test files on four worker processes at the same time. Each test gets a default limit of 15 seconds, not the runner default of 5 seconds. A test that needs more still sets its own, longer limit.

The longer limit does not hide a slow test or a frozen test. A test that hangs still fails, only 10 seconds later. A check that runs past its own time limit is a fail of the check infrastructure, not of the code (#ms-fail-cause), so the run time of the whole suite is the number to protect.

Each worker is a separate process, and each test file starts with fresh globals in its worker. The test setup therefore runs once per worker, not once per run.
EOF
cat > /tmp/why-werk-test-runner-parallel.md <<'EOF'
Run in one process, the unit tests take most of the time that the build loop gives one check, so a slow machine fails the check for time alone. Parallel workers make the run shorter. But the workers compete for the machine, so a test that starts many processes in sequence runs past a short per-test limit.
EOF

card werk-mc-park-unpark  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
An un-park keeps a live process, and resumes a stopped one at once
why: A parked conversation whose process still runs has lost nothing, so a restart would only cost time. A conversation whose process was stopped must be back before the person types, so the resume starts at the click and not at the next message.

The page tells the server each time a conversation is parked or un-parked. Only the server knows whether the conversation's process still runs. To avoid a second process for one conversation, an un-park of a conversation with a live process changes nothing on the server. To avoid a wait at the next message, an un-park of a conversation with no live process and a known session starts a new process at once, and that process resumes the session (see #werk-resume). A conversation with no session yet starts nothing on un-park. Its first message starts a fresh process.

Example: conversations A and B. B has the session s-b. A has never sent a message.
1. B is parked. Its process still runs. The person clicks B in the '…' menu. B's chip comes back, and no process starts.
2. B is parked again and stays idle past the idle limit. The idle check kills its process (see #werk-mc-reap).
3. The person clicks B in the menu. The server starts a process at once, and it resumes s-b. The person types into a conversation that is already running.
4. A is un-parked. No process starts. A's first message starts a fresh process.

```
un-park B
  live process?  yes -> keep it, start nothing              (step 1)
                 no  -> session known?
                          yes -> start now, resume s-b      (step 3)
                          no  -> start nothing              (step 4)
```

/**
 * The conversation manager (#werk-chat, #werk-chat-stdin, #werk-invoke). Each conversation
 * tab has one Claude Code child in the chat role, spoken to over stream-json. The child lives
 * across many messages: each message is one more user line on its stdin, one turn.
 *
 * The child runs one turn at a time. The manager keeps the turns that were sent and have not
 * ended, in the order they were sent, and gives each part of the reply to the oldest of them.
 * The end of a turn closes it, and the next one starts (#werk-chat-turn-id). A child that exits
 * ends every open turn with the exit, so no turn waits forever, and the next message starts a
 * new child.
 *
 * Each tab keeps its session id, from the init event of its child, and its home card
 * (#werk-mc-split). A tab opened from another tab records the session of that tab at the
 * moment it opens: the fork point. Its child then starts on that session with the fork
 * option, so it shares the parent's cached prefix and leaves the parent untouched
 * (#werk-mc-fork). A tab opened empty, or from a tab that has no session yet, has no parent
 * session, and its child starts a new one. The first turn of an opened tab names its home card.
 *
 * A tab can be parked (#werk-mc-park). Its child lives on: a parked tab is not closed. An idle
 * check runs every `checkMs` and kills the child of each parked tab that has had no turn open
 * and no agent activity for `idleMs` (#werk-mc-reap, #werk-mc-reap-sweep). A message wakes the
 * tab. Each child after the first of a tab with a session resumes that session (#werk-resume),
 * and an un-park of a tab whose child is gone starts that resumed child at once
 * (#werk-mc-park-unpark).
 *
 * The manager reports a status per tab to the status sink each time it changes (#werk-mc-live):
 * running while a turn is open or a background agent of the child runs (#werk-mc-bgagents),
 * the first permission ask of the child that has no answer, and dead from an exit that werk
 * did not cause until the tab's next child starts. A tab keeps its own asks, and an answer goes
 * to that tab's child alone (#werk-mc-asks). A child that exits takes its asks and its
 * background agents with it.
 *
 * Each new session a tab's child reports goes to the session sink, so the conversations log
 * lists it (#werk-mc-shared-convo-log). Nothing a tab says reaches another tab's child: a tab
 * reads a sibling from its transcript when it needs it (#werk-mc-shared).
 */

Each held-out step comes from the brief of one ticket, its source ticket. To keep one hard step from blocking unrelated fixes, a red held-out run groups its red steps by source ticket and files one follow-up ticket per group. Each follow-up cites the cards of its own source ticket and has its own retry cap. A red step that an open follow-up already carries files nothing again.

Example:

- Tickets P and Q are merged. Run R turns step P.2 red, and steps Q.1 and Q.4 red.

1. R files follow-up F1 with step P.2. F1 cites the cards of P.
2. R files follow-up F2 with steps Q.1 and Q.4. F2 cites the cards of Q.
3. F2 stops at its cap. F1 still builds and merges.
4. A later run turns Q.1 red again while F2 is open. F2 already carries Q.1, so nothing is filed.

```
run R:  P.2 ✗   Q.1 ✗   Q.4 ✗
         │        └───┬───┘
         ▼            ▼
        F1 (P)       F2 (Q)      ✗ = red step, (X) = source ticket
```
EOF

card werk-test-runner-parallel  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
The unit tests run on parallel workers, with a per-test time limit that allows for the shared load
why: Run in one process, the unit tests take most of the time that the build loop gives one check, so a slow machine fails the check for time alone. Parallel workers make the run shorter. But the workers compete for the machine, so a test that starts many processes in sequence runs past a short per-test limit.

To keep the unit test run well inside the time limit of one check, the test command runs the test files on four worker processes at the same time. Each test gets a default limit of 15 seconds, not the runner default of 5 seconds. A test that needs more still sets its own, longer limit.

The merge loop drives one run: a temporary merge worktree, a guarded branch move, and a stop when a build stays red
why: The merge loop has to be safe to resume and must never overwrite a run tree that moved under it.

- Starting the merge loop on a planned subtree is the person's trigger for its tickets. Starting it again resumes.
- The merge queue merges the ticket's branch in a detached worktree and runs the ticket's own checks there.
- The main line moves only from the value it had when the merge started, so a main line that changed in between is never overwritten (#st-plan-main). A checkout of the main line moves with it by a fast-forward. A checkout whose local changes block that fast-forward stops the loop, and nothing moves.
- After a red merge, the next build starts from the ticket's old branch when that branch sits on top of the main line.
- A ticket's retry cap counts passes across all its builds, so it also bounds the trips between the builder and the merge queue.
- A build that stays red stops the loop as stuck.
- Every start of the loop writes the feature tier event to the board log first (#werk-loop-tier).
- G2 belongs to the main line's tip: a later merge opens it again. Only a person passes it (#st-gates).

The pie shows the context in use over the context window. The model reports both, so neither is a guess.

- The numerator is the usage of the latest assistant message: input tokens + output tokens + cache-read tokens + cache-creation tokens. One assistant message is one API call, so its usage is the size of the conversation at that call.
- The denominator is the context window size from the turn's final result. Only the window size is read from there. The final result sums the usage of every call of the turn, so a turn with ten tool calls reports ten times the real size.

The pie is blue (the proto colour) under 33%, yellow (the open colour) from 33%, and red (the stale colour) from 66%. It is a CSS conic gradient on a 16px button, with no canvas and no chart library.

An un-park keeps a live process, and resumes a stopped one at once
why: A parked conversation whose process still runs has lost nothing, so a restart would only cost time. A conversation whose process was stopped must be back before the person types, so the resume starts at the click and not at the next message.

The page tells the server each time a conversation is parked or un-parked. Only the server knows whether the conversation's process still runs. To avoid a second process for one conversation, an un-park of a conversation with a live process changes nothing on the server. To avoid a wait at the next message, an un-park of a conversation with no live process and a known session starts a new process at once, and that process resumes the session (see #werk-resume). A conversation with no session yet starts nothing on un-park. Its first message starts a fresh process.

Each reviewer's role name carries its quality area
why: The reviewers of a pass run at the same time, one per quality area, so a test cannot tell them apart by launch order or by prompt text. A test must still script a finding for one area only. A role name per area lets the fake give each reviewer its own reply.

A reviewer's role name is the word reviewer, a dash, and a short fixed word for its quality area (see #lp-prod-review for the areas): reviewer-design, reviewer-security, and so on. A new area gets a new role name when it is added. Every reviewer still lives for one pass, like every agent that is not a chat agent (see #werk-chat-fake-role).

Example:

- A test scripts reply F, one HIGH finding, for reviewer-security. It scripts reply E, with no finding, for every other area.

1. The pass starts one reviewer per area, all at once. Each carries its own reviewer-<area> name.
2. The fake reads reviewer-security and plays F. The other reviewers play E.
3. The pass fails at the review, and the failure names the security finding.
4. If the test scripts E for every area, no reviewer finds anything, and the pass goes green at the review.

```
reviewer-design           -> E
reviewer-maintainability  -> E
reviewer-tests            -> E
reviewer-security         -> F (HIGH)  -> pass red at review
reviewer-performance      -> E

reviewer-<area>   the role name of the reviewer for one area
F                 the scripted reply with one HIGH finding
E                 the scripted reply with no finding
```

card werk-board-control-archive-ends-build  [decided]
The builder loop ends its own build when it reads that its ticket is archived
why: A build can run from the merge loop or from a single build command, and only the builder loop is present in both. When the builder loop reads the board itself, an archive ends every build the same way, with no second process that has to notice it.

While a build runs, its builder loop reads the board about once a second. When it finds its ticket archived during a pass, it stops the agent of that pass, commits nothing of the pass, runs no checks, records no retry, and ends. An archive that comes while the checks or the grader of the last pass run also ends the build: nothing of the build merges, even a pass that ended green. In every case the worktree folder goes and the ticket's branch stays.

A merge loop that started the build merges nothing of it and goes on with its other tickets. The archive ends one build. It is not a stop of the merge loop, so no other ticket moves back to ready.

Example:

- Ticket T "Draw the board" is in building. The agent of its pass 2 runs.
- Ticket U "Save the log" builds beside T in the same merge loop.
- A person archives T on the board.

1. The board log gets the archive. T leaves the columns.
2. Within about a second, the builder loop of T reads the board and sees T archived.
3. It stops the pass 2 agent. The board no longer shows T as running.
4. The builder loop of T ends. The branch of T stays. Nothing of T merges.
5. The merge loop goes on. U builds and merges as before.

=================== werk-mc-shared-convo-log
card werk-mc-shared-convo-log  [decided]
Each conversation session is one line in an append-only conversations log beside the map log
why: The server appends one line for each session a tab reports and never rewrites a line, so a session stays listable after its tab moves on to a new one. A store that kept one current session per tab would overwrite the old session.

To keep every past session listable, the server appends one line to a conversations log in the same folder as the map log. It appends the line each time a tab's agent reports a session. A line holds the tab name, the session id, the home card when the tab has one (see #werk-mc-split), and the parent session when the tab is a fork (see #werk-mc-fork). No line is ever rewritten. The list of conversations folds the lines into one entry per session id, so a second line for a session the log holds already adds no entry.

A plain restart resumes the same session, so the list keeps one entry for it (see #werk-resume). A tab gets a new session under its old name only when its stored session no longer resolves at a start, or when the server starts the first tab fresh on purpose. In those cases the old session stays in the log.

Example. These things exist:

- Tab main, whose agent reports session s-1.
- Tab map-hash, a fork of s-1 with home card #map-hash, whose agent reports session s-2.

1. Tab main reports s-1. The log gains the line main s-1.
2. Tab map-hash reports s-2. The log gains the line map-hash s-2, home #map-hash, parent s-1.
3. The server restarts and tab main resumes s-1. The list still shows one entry for s-1.
4. At the next restart s-1 no longer resolves, so tab main reports a new session s-3. The log gains the line main s-3.
5. The list shows three conversations: s-1, s-2 and s-3. Both s-1 and s-3 carry the tab name main.

```
step  event                          line appended to the conversations log
1     main reports s-1          -->  main      s-1
2     map-hash reports s-2      -->  map-hash  s-2  home #map-hash  parent s-1
3     restart, main resumes s-1 -->  (no new entry: s-1 is in the log already)
4     restart, s-1 is gone,
      main reports s-3          -->  main      s-3

list:  s-1 (main)   s-2 (map-hash)   s-3 (main)
```

       why: The log records each conversation under the home card that this card gives it.
  -> depends_on      werk-mc-recall  A tab lists its sibling conversations and reads any one of them
       why: The list and read operations of this card find each conversation in this log.
  -> depends_on      werk-mc-fork  Fork the session, do not start it empty
       why: A fork is its own session with a parent session, as this card decides, so a log line records that parent.
  -> depends_on      werk-resume  A restart resumes the conversation
       why: A restart resumes the stored session, so its line adds no new entry; only the fallback to a new session that this card defines adds one.
  -> refines         werk-mc-shared  Cross-tab memory is pulled from the session logs, not pushed into context
  <- alternative_to  werk-mc-shared-convo-log:opt0  One folder per tab, holding a file with the tab's current session id

why: Run in one process, the unit tests take most of the time that the build loop gives one check, so a slow machine fails the check for time alone. Parallel workers make the run shorter. To keep the unit test run well inside the time limit of one check, the test command runs the test files on four worker processes at the same time. Each test gets a default limit of 15 seconds, not the runner default of 5 seconds. A test that needs more still sets its own, longer limit.

=== werk-mc-tabs-step-wrap
card werk-mc-tabs-step-wrap  [decided]
A step past the last chip goes to the first, and a step before the first goes to the last
why: Stepping is the secondary way to switch tabs, used to cycle through a short strip. A step that stops at an end does nothing on the next press, so the person must check where they are. A wrap always moves, the way browser tab stepping does.

To keep every step press useful, the strip treats its chips as a ring. The next step from the last chip focuses the first chip, and the previous step from the first chip focuses the last chip. A strip with one chip stays where it is. A step keeps each tab's own map position, so the map moves to the card of the chip that gets focus.

Example, with three chips in insertion order:

- chip 1 "the map", at card fold
- chip 2 "#fold", at card log
- chip 3 "#log", at card map-hash

1. Chip 3 has focus. The person steps to the next chip. Chip 1 gets focus, and the map moves to fold.
2. The person steps to the previous chip. Chip 3 gets focus again, and the map moves to map-hash.
3. Only chip 1 is open. A step in either direction leaves chip 1 focused, and nothing moves.

```
 next:     [1] -> [2] -> [3] --+
            ^                  |
            +------------------+
 previous: the same ring, the other way
```

  -> refines         werk-mc-tabs  A tab strip of card-id chips, in the bottom control cluster
  -> depends_on      werk-mc-keys  Cmd+1 to Cmd+5 select a tab by position
       why: The wrap is how the previous-chip and next-chip step keys behave, and #werk-mc-keys defines those keys as the secondary way to switch tabs.

/**
 * The held-out set. See #lp-prod-heldout, #st-validate-heldout.
 *
 * Three parts, each its own agent, none of them the builder:
 *
 *   - The step author (#lp-heldout-author) writes Given/When/Then steps (#lp-heldout-steps)
 *     from the ticket's brief, while the builder builds. It gets no tools: it cannot read the
 *     code, and the steps it answers with are stored by this file in .werk/heldout/<run>/,
 *     outside every worktree a builder works in.
 *   - The binder (#lp-heldout-binder) turns every step of the run's merged tickets
 *     (#st-heldout-merged-only) into a test on the merged tree, runs them, and reports each step: pass, fail (a missing feature), or binder-error.
 *     It works in a throwaway worktree; its tests never reach the main line. A binder that
 *     changes a file outside its test directory has fitted the code to the test, so its whole
 *     report is void.
 *   - A failed step files a follow-up ticket whose text holds that step, word for word, and
 *     no other step and no test code (#lp-heldout-feedback).
 *
 * Each steps file records the version of each card it was written from. Before a run, the
 * step author rewrites or drops the steps of a ticket whose source card changed since
 * (#st-heldout-step-fresh).
 */

/** Every stored step of the run, in ticket order. */
export function readSteps(cwd: string, run: string): Step[] {
  const dir = heldoutDir(cwd, run)
  if (!existsSync(dir)) return []
  return readdirSync(dir)
    .filter((f) => f.endsWith('.steps.md'))
    .sort()
    .flatMap((f) => {
      const num = f.replace(/\.steps\.md$/, '')
      return readFileSync(join(dir, f), 'utf8')
        .split(/\n\s*\n/)
        .map((t) => t.trim())
        .filter(Boolean)
        .map((text, i) => ({ id: `${num}.${i + 1}`, ticket: `${run}/${num}`, text }))
    })
}

The silence clock starts at the agent's first event
why: An agent process takes time to start before it writes anything, and that time grows under load. Counting it as silence cancels a healthy agent when the silence limit is short. A start that never ends is still caught by the wall-clock limit of the session.

The silence limit measures the time between two events of a session. Its clock starts when the agent writes its first event, and starts again at each event after that. Before the first event, only the wall-clock limit of the session applies (see #al-sample-budget).

Example, with a silence limit of 60 s and a wall-clock limit of 600 s:

- Agent A "starts slowly": under load it takes 90 s to start. It writes its first event, then stops.
- Agent B "runs a long build": it writes a tool call event at 5 s. The build runs for 300 s, then the result comes.
- Agent C "never starts": it writes no event at all.

 * A stand-in for the `claude` CLI, put first on PATH by setup.ts. It speaks just enough of
 * `--input-format stream-json` / `--output-format stream-json` for agent.ts to run a turn,
 * and records what it was asked so a test can read it back.
 *
 * Steered by environment variables, read at spawn time:
 *
 *   FAKE_CLAUDE_LOG      file: one JSON line per launch ({argv}) and per stdin line ({stdin})
 *   FAKE_CLAUDE_MODE     ok (default) | crash | gone | ask | hang
 *                          ok    init, then one assistant reply and a result per user turn
 *                          crash read one turn, write FAKE_CLAUDE_STDERR, exit 1, no init
 *                          gone  with --resume: "No conversation found with session ID", exit 1;
 *                                without it: ok
 *                          ask   per user turn, one can_use_tool request; the answer is logged,
 *                                then the turn ends with a result
 *                          hang  init, then never finish a turn
 *   FAKE_CLAUDE_SESSION  the session id init reports (default sess-<pid>)
 *   FAKE_CLAUDE_STDERR   what crash writes (default "boom")
 *   FAKE_CLAUDE_SUGGEST  JSON permission_suggestions for ask mode
 *
 * Launched with `--print <prompt>` and no stream-json input — the way sample.ts and
 * prototype.ts call it — it logs the launch and exits 0 with no output.
 */
import { appendFileSync } from 'node:fs'
import { createInterface } from 'node:readline'

const argv = process.argv.slice(2)
const env = process.env
const record = (entry: unknown) => {
  if (env.FAKE_CLAUDE_LOG) appendFileSync(env.FAKE_CLAUDE_LOG, JSON.stringify(entry) + '\n')
}
const out = (event: unknown) => process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify(event) + '\n')

record({ argv, pid: process.pid })

if (!argv.includes('--input-format')) process.exit(0)

const resume = argv.includes('--resume') ? argv[argv.indexOf('--resume') + 1] : null
let mode = env.FAKE_CLAUDE_MODE ?? 'ok'
if (mode === 'gone' && !resume) mode = 'ok'

card st-build-ticket-hand-off  [decided]
When a build of one ticket ends, its ticket leaves the building column
why: The building column shows only tickets that a session builds now. So a build that ends moves its ticket out by how it ended: a green build to merging, where the next merge loop merges its branch, and a build red at the retry cap back to ready with the reason, where the ticket waits for its next build.

To keep the building column to tickets that a session builds now (#werk-board-columns), a build of one ticket that the merge loop did not start moves its ticket out of building when it ends. Where the ticket goes depends on how the build ends. A green build moves the ticket to merging, and the board records the branch that holds the green work. The build does not merge that branch: the merge loop owns every change to the main line (#st-build-run), and its next run on the ticket's subtree merges the branch before it starts a new build. A build that stays red at the retry cap moves the ticket back to ready, with the reason, the same as a ticket of a stopped merge loop (#st-build-stop-ready). An archive also ends a build, and its ticket leaves the columns (#werk-board-control-archive-ends-build).

Example, with two tickets in ready:

- Ticket 3 "The export writes one file per order".
- Ticket 4 "The import reads a file of orders".

1. The person builds ticket 3. While pass 1 runs, ticket 3 stays in building.
2. Pass 1 goes green. Ticket 3 moves to merging, with its build branch.
3. The person builds ticket 3 again. The build refuses: ticket 3 is in merging, not in ready.
4. The person builds ticket 4. Every pass stays red until the retry cap. Ticket 4 goes back to ready with the reason "red at the retry cap".
5. The person starts the run of the subtree. The merge loop merges the branch of ticket 3 before it starts any build.

```
ready --build--> building --green-------------> merging --merge loop--> done
  ^                 |
  +-----------------+
   red at the retry cap: back to ready, with the reason

building = a session builds the ticket now
```

The line between the two tabs: Flow shows what is counted from map cards — statuses, marks, edges, and the status loop (#vi-flowtab). Measure shows what is counted from the pipeline log, the conversations and the background jobs: cost, failures, waits, and the gauges of metric kill criteria.

A time window at the top applies to every panel (#vi-measure-scope). A rail on the left lists the panel questions in groups. A red dot in the rail marks a question whose panel has a mark outside its band. The main column opens with one row of kill-criterion gauges (#vi-measure-kill), then the panel groups cost, failures and waits.

**Rules for every panel.**
- **One question.** The question is the panel title.
- **Transform first.** A panel shows a fold over the logs, not raw events: per unit of size, a distribution (median, 90th percentile, maximum), a window, or a ratio.
- **Legend.** Every panel names its marks, its lines and its band.
- **Colour marks the outlier.** A mark outside the reference band has its own colour, so a person finds it without a click or a hover.
- **Drill-down.** A mark opens the items behind it: the tickets, cards, and transcripts. A card opens on the map by the click rule of the flow tables (#vi-flowtab-click).
- **Reference band.** Each panel compares against its own history (#vi-flow-ms-ref).
- **Live.** A panel redraws when the pipeline log or the decision log gets an event.
- **Look.** The panel images on the child cards show layout and marks, with made-up data. The type, colours and spacing follow the visual system of the rest of the tool.

A panel that compares two pipeline variants waits for the replay set (#ms-replay).

  - A bar per run: red for a timeout, amber for another failure, grey for a clean run.
